title: A year with The Vegetable Guru
subtitle: Reader journeys and a practical final-edit plan
status: Proposals for John’s review — no book changes made
verdict: The book works well as a practical crop reference. Most decisions can be made from the existing two-page spreads and Troubles pages. The final pass should improve the joins: interpreting dates, recognising the stage of a job, moving between crops, and finding advice by task.
scope: Three complete January–December simulations, plus a cooler northern-site stress test. These are evidence-backed role plays, not interviews, observed user tests or growing trials. The current imperial preview was reviewed; this is not a fresh validation of every horticultural claim in all 44 guides.
recommendation: Make seven focused editorial improvements, settle three specific copy decisions, and leave the book’s structure, page count and two-page crop format intact. The optional ideas can wait.

strengths.title: The second page earns its place
strengths.text: The practical pages usually resolve the uncertainty left by a calendar or quick fact: seed versus sets, direct versus indoor sowing, heated versus unheated cover, and observable harvest cues.

strengths.title: Troubles helps the reader take action
strengths.text: Crop-specific links lead to recognition, action and prevention. The allium pages distinguish leek moth from leaf miner; the tomato pages distinguish moisture disorders from pests. These routes should be preserved.

strengths.title: Winter growing is already substantially covered
strengths.text: Kale, leeks, parsnips, sprouting broccoli and storage crops support an experienced reader’s full year. Useful succession advice already exists in the kale, garlic, turnip and Oriental-leaf guides.

strengths.title: The techniques are practical and conditional
strengths.text: Starting small, checking soil and weather, hardening plants, watering according to need and adapting rotation to small areas all work. A new beginner chapter or fixed monthly prescription is not needed.

actions.title: Make the calendar key describe what the colours actually mean
actions.problem: Muted months are described as options for warmer climates. The source also uses less-usual dates for protected starts, particular varieties and overwintering methods. Bright sowing months can include raising indoors. A reader can mistake a sowing window for an outdoor planting instruction.
actions.change: Revise the existing explanation and the “warmer climates” sublabel. Describe less-usual dates as conditional options, direct readers to the crop’s Sowing & planting instructions, and distinguish sowing from transplanting. Retain both colours and all source dates.
actions.evidence: Carrot has a protected late route; lettuce has protected early and overwintering routes; greenhouse cucumber distinguishes heated and unheated starts on its practical page. All three reader journeys encountered this mismatch.
actions.space: Replace current words within the approved peach key panel. No new calendar, graphic or page.
actions.check: Read the revised key against carrot, lettuce, courgette and greenhouse cucumber. Check the actual page 9 proof and both-unit examples.

actions.title: Separate sowing, planting and planting depth
actions.problem: The greenhouse page says to use “earlier planting dates” for plants raised for later outdoor planting. Celeriac’s “Depth” is a crown planting position, while asparagus’s “Depth” is seed depth beside a crop primarily described from crowns.
actions.change: On p161, distinguish an earlier protected sowing/raising window from the later outdoor planting conditions. On p16 use “Planting depth”; on p88 use “Seed depth”. Preserve the existing methods, measurements and condition checks.
actions.evidence: P157 already says to delay in cold or wet weather. Outdoor cucumber and tomato have their own frost/warmth conditions. Canonical celeriac has no numeric sowing depth; its printed depth comes from planting_depth. Asparagus has separate seed and crown instructions.
actions.space: One sentence replacement and two short label changes. No extra calendar row or altered planting method.
actions.check: Check label wrapping in both units and consistency with the facing practical pages. Do not globally relabel all 44 guides without checking their field meanings.

actions.title: Restore exact source values and an important qualification
actions.problem: Greenhouse tomato prints germination warmth near 68°F (20°C in the corresponding print draft), while the canonical field is around 64°F / 18°C. The leek-moth cut-back instruction omits the condition that enough growing season remains for possible recovery.
actions.change: Align the tomato germination number with its exact canonical value, preserving context. Restore the remaining-season qualification to the leek-moth action; recovery should remain possible rather than promised.
actions.evidence: The tomato mismatch predates the latest two-page trial: its expected and proposed copy both contain 68°F/20°C. This is a source-fidelity correction, not a claim that 68°F is a dangerous germination temperature. The leek qualification matters to a late-autumn lookup.
actions.space: One numeric substitution and a short qualification. Retain the current two-page tomato design and the existing leek treatment context.
actions.check: Trace the change through the separate print copy and recheck both-unit affected proofs. Keep the canonical records unchanged.

actions.title: Make a few seasonal handovers easier to act on
actions.problem: The reader often knows how to do the operation but not when to prepare for it: leek transplanting lacks a month range; the autumn greenhouse paragraph begins with clearing summer crops; some useful tomato stage cues have been compressed to “as needed” or “near season’s end”.
actions.change: First restore May–July beside the leek’s pencil-thick transplant cue, keeping readiness and conditions. Then add a short p161 reminder to raise suitable replacements within their sowing window before space is cleared, with crop references. If space permits, restore lettuce’s qualified August/early-September protected overwintering route. On p83 prioritise the source’s cold-night cue and true-leaf/root-fill cues over vague warmth or “as needed” wording; the often-August unheated stopping example is a lower priority. A protected late carrot example is also optional after the key is fixed.
actions.evidence: These instructions already exist in source records. Kale and garlic already explain useful succession, so the issue is a few incomplete links, not absence of winter or follow-on growing throughout the book.
actions.space: Replace vague or repeated words first. P83 is already dense: do not install every candidate if it costs readability or useful table rows. No extra seasonal page.
actions.check: Keep “about 10°C/50°F” as a tomato cold-night cue, not a universal crop threshold; keep lettuce variety/protection conditions. Check both units and the complete facing spreads.

actions.title: Make the rotation family list useful for an ordinary small crop selection
actions.problem: The five-row list helps with brassicas, alliums, peas/beans, potatoes/tomatoes and carrots/parsnips. It does not tell a beginner where lettuce or courgettes belong; beetroot, leaf beet and spinach are another common omission.
actions.change: Add compact examples for the beet/spinach/leaf-beet, cucumber/squash/courgette and lettuce/chicory/endive families. Extend existing rows with useful book crops such as peppers/aubergines and celery/celeriac/fennel. Keep the flexible small-area approach, permanent-crop exception and persistent-disease warning.
actions.evidence: Two of the novice’s five chosen crops are absent from the table. The family relationships are supported by the existing research trail, Garden Organic’s family table and the University of Saskatchewan table. The foreign source is used for membership, not UK planting dates or a fixed rotation interval.
actions.space: Reallocate space within p156, preferably reducing the large three-crop example before reducing text size. This is a proposed local layout adjustment, not an approved replacement.
actions.check: Validate every added family member, include the useful common annual crops, and check the actual one-page proof. Do not imply the table is exhaustive unless it is.

actions.title: Add a few routes for readers who start with a job or familiar crop name
actions.problem: Chillies are covered but have no direct index entry. An experienced reader looking for succession, winter harvesting or storage must already know which crop passages contain the answer.
actions.change: Add “Chillies → Peppers (capsicums)”. Add a small, curated Succession/follow-on route to existing examples such as kale p41, Oriental leaves p59 and garlic p62. Consider Winter harvesting and Storage only if each gives a short useful selection, not a long indiscriminate list.
actions.evidence: The combined capsicum spread includes Demon Red and Habanero Orange and chilli care. Existing winter and storage instructions are strong; this action exposes them rather than duplicating them.
actions.space: One definite alias plus a few carefully chosen entries within the existing four pages. Preserve plain structure and readable type.
actions.check: Use destination identities rather than hard-coded folios. Verify alphabetical order, see-reference targets and actual index fit. Keep vegetable “See also” links restricted to pages mentioning that vegetable.

actions.title: Replace a little weak or repeated text with more useful information
actions.problem: Lettuce’s first-page slug risk card is a long, opaque prevention paragraph rather than recognition signs. The courgette final tips repeat picking advice but omit ordinary crop clearance. The sowing page assumes a novice knows “drill” and “module”.
actions.change: Use the existing lettuce signs, “Ragged leaves; slime trails”, for its recognition card; keep control on the practical/Troubles pages. Replace the repeated courgette tip with its source-backed healthy-crop clearance instruction, retaining the diseased-material distinction. Add very short plain-language glosses for a drill and module cells at first use; explain a station where it occurs.
actions.evidence: The lettuce record already separates signs and control; no efficacy claim needs inventing. Courgette harvesting[5] already supplies the close-down advice. Existing sowing illustrations help, so only a few explanatory words are needed.
locators: Current p157 Direct into the bed / Start under cover
actions.space: Lettuce becomes shorter. Courgette is a substitution. Use small glosses within p157; only shorten the optional mixed-salad experiment if genuinely necessary.
actions.check: Retain pictures, conditions and body text size. Inspect the changed crop spreads in both units. Do not turn this into a glossary chapter.

decisions.title: Narrow the compost-input claim and settle what “pet litter” means
decisions.problem: The lead accepts anything of organic origin, names pet litter and says the bin takes all you throw at it. The same page excludes some materials, and the Troubles pages exclude specific infected debris from home compost. The absolute wording is already inconsistent within the book.
decisions.evidence: John’s local manuscript explicitly includes cat/dog litter with faeces (lines 2011–2025). Garden Organic and EPA exclude cat litter/pet waste from ordinary home composting. Earlier research notes flagged the issue, but the current approved copy contains the phrase; the old note is not authority to silently revert approved text.
decisions.recommendation: Replace the sweeping claim with suitable garden and kitchen materials and a clear exceptions cue. For this beginner food-growing guide, my recommendation is to omit the broad pet-litter example unless John wants a separately qualified treatment. Agree that narrow scope before editing; do not present a general home bin as a specialist pet-waste process.
decisions.space: A shorter replacement lead, not a new compost chapter.
decisions.confidence: Confirmed scope conflict; author decision needed for the local-source disagreement.

decisions.title: Clarify the carrot compost warning
decisions.problem: The key-risk card warns about manure or compost shortly before sowing, while the introduction permits compost-filled no-dig beds and the techniques permit planting into mature compost. The reader cannot tell whether the warning concerns fresh material, incorporation, maturity or a fine sowing cover.
decisions.evidence: The broad wording is in the canonical carrot record as well as print. The shared Troubles record distinguishes fresh manure and stones/compaction; it is not evidence that the recent layout work invented the conflict.
decisions.recommendation: Settle the intended distinction, then harmonise only the short printed warning and necessary related phrasing. The likely useful distinction is fresh/unfinished additions versus suitably mature compost, with location and use made clear. This remains a proposal until the source conflict is resolved.
decisions.space: One focused risk-card clarification; no new no-dig debate or revised crop method.
decisions.confidence: Confirmed internal ambiguity; source meaning requires John’s decision.

decisions.title: Make Greyhound’s printed group agree with its description
decisions.problem: Greyhound appears under “Spring cabbages”, immediately described as a traditional pointed summer cabbage. That is confusing when the reader chooses a variety for a season.
decisions.evidence: The master has Greyhound in both SPRING and SUMMER groups at rank 9 with the same summer short description. The current renderer sorts by rank and deduplicates names; this tie retains the first group. The spring entry’s longer text describes late-winter/early-spring raising for a June cut.
decisions.recommendation: For this selected printed row, use a group and description that agree on the intended early/summer crop. Preserve both canonical entries and resolve their scope separately if requested. This is not evidence for a global variety-deduplication change.
decisions.space: Short label change, subject to agreeing which seasonal route the row represents.
decisions.confidence: Confirmed reader-facing label mismatch; classification choice remains for review.

optional.title: One small worked succession example
optional.text: A single source-linked example could show that the next crop is raised before the first clears: for example, the existing kale route after an early crop, with its sowing and planting qualifications. Prefer a compact callout or reference within p156 if the revised family table leaves room. Do not replace the approved finger/leaf bed illustrations on p149 for this audit: those have a distinct purpose, and strong succession examples already exist on pp41,59,62. A full annual planner is not justified.

optional.title: A short holiday-care reminder
optional.text: If a line can be spared, prompt the reader to arrange moisture checks, vent operation and picking while away. Ordinary care is already explained, and John’s manuscript discusses holiday watering. No equipment list, new irrigation chapter or guarantee of unattended care is needed.

do_not_expand: Keep the two-page vegetable spreads, body type size, three-section structure, facing contents and established section starts.
Do not add a complete monthly calendar, universal north/south date offsets, a separate winter-growing chapter or household-yield promises.
Do not claim succession, winter storage, unheated growing, direct sowing, harvesting cues or ordinary feeding guidance are absent: they are substantially present.
Do not cut varieties or pest rows to make room for every optional sentence. Use replacements and remove genuine repetition first.

Do not remove rare/reportable pest entries merely because they are uncommon. Uncertain identities such as Clayburn or Parsnip Rust Fungus remain a separate, recorded research question, not an automatic deletion list.

Do not silently alter original JSON, approved proofs or retained sources. Future print changes should stay source-linked, with any authorised shared-copy save using the guarded writer and exact backups.

batches.name: 1. Agree scope and remove ambiguity
batches.result: Decisions recorded and a small set of precise wording/label changes ready for highlighted proofs.

batches.name: 2. Improve the joins between pages
batches.result: Targeted timing, family-map, navigation and useful-text substitutions; reject additions that cannot fit comfortably.

batches.name: 3. Check changed proofs, then assemble once
batches.result: Inspect actual changed pages and facing spreads in metric and imperial, retain body size and two-page guides, verify references and source preservation. Show highlights for review. After approval, remove only those highlights and update the full preview once.

acceptance: A novice can distinguish sowing from outdoor planting using the key and facing guide.
The leek and autumn-salad handovers can be planned before the bed or greenhouse is empty.
Chillies and selected follow-on/winter tasks have accurate, short index routes.
Carrot and compost wording no longer pull the reader in conflicting directions after John’s decisions.
Numeric source values, qualifiers, useful diagnoses, original source bytes and approved design constraints are preserved.
Actual changed proofs fit in both units without smaller body text; no new page-count or facing-page problem is introduced.

sources.title: RHS — Planning a vegetable garden
sources.use: Reader-task framing: household preferences, available space/time, avoiding gluts, repeated crops and a practical plan. Supports the tasks tested, not a finding that this book lacks them.

sources.title: Garden Organic — Plan to grow
sources.use: Reader-task framing: manageable choices, repeat versus once-only crops, and planning winter supplies ahead. Reinforces the handover test rather than demanding a new chapter.

sources.title: Garden Organic — Silver and Gold growing resource, family table
sources.use: Family membership only. Existing book research already cites this table; no fixed rotation prescription imported.

sources.title: University of Saskatchewan — Rotating your vegetables
sources.use: Independent comparison for vegetable-family membership, including beet/spinach/chard, cucurbits, carrot relatives and potato relatives. Not used for UK timings.

sources.title: Garden Organic — What can I compost?
sources.use: Distinguishes vegetarian-pet bedding from excluded cat litter/dog faeces in ordinary garden composting. This conflicts substantively with the local manuscript; it is evidence for a decision, not an automatic override.

sources.title: US EPA — Composting at home
sources.use: Independent backyard-compost guidance excludes pet waste and cat litter. Used only for that ordinary-home-compost scope.

sources.title: A novice’s planning question — GardeningUK
sources.use: Anecdotal context only: a beginner asks about crop choice, succession and quantities, with online communities/video among suggested resources. Not representative research or authority for horticultural changes.
